title: Switching Accountants Mid-Year: How to Move Your Books Without Losing History
seoTitle: Switching Accountants Mid-Year: A 2026 Handover Guide
metaDescription: Changing accountants mid-year? The handover pack to demand, why opening balances decide everything, portal access to reclaim, and a clean switching sequence.
excerpt: Changing accountants is easy; handing over the books is not. Here is a sequence that keeps your history intact — when to switch, the documents to demand from the outgoing firm, why opening balances decide everything, and the access to reclaim on day one.

faq.question: When is the best time to change accountants?
faq.answer: The start of a financial year, once the previous year is filed, because the closing balances are settled and become the new firm's opening set. The start of a quarter with returns already filed is a workable second choice.

faq.question: Can my old accountant refuse to hand over my records?
faq.answer: The books and records of the business belong to the business. Disputes usually concern the firm's own working papers rather than your records, and unpaid fees are a separate matter to settle on their own terms. If a handover stalls, put the request in writing with a date.

faq.question: What is the single most important document to get?
faq.answer: The trial balance as at the handover date, signed off by the outgoing firm. It is what the new books open from, and every later disagreement about the balance sheet traces back to whether it was agreed or assumed.

faq.question: Do I have to tell the tax department I changed accountants?
faq.answer: There is no separate notification for changing who does your bookkeeping. What does need updating is anything where the firm was listed — authorised signatory, portal contact details and any registered representative — so check each portal on the handover date.

faq.question: How long should I keep records from the old firm?
faq.answer: Longer than the switch. As a general guide, six years from the end of the relevant assessment year for income tax, six years from the annual return filing date for GST, and eight years from the end of the financial year for a company. Keep your own backup, not theirs.

bodyHtml:
Most businesses change accountants for undramatic reasons. Replies got slower. The filing was made on the last possible day for the third year running. The firm grew and you got handed to someone junior. Or nothing went wrong at all — you simply outgrew a one-person setup and want monthly numbers instead of an annual scramble.

The switch itself is rarely the hard part. What goes wrong is the handover: a set of books that stops on one date and restarts on another with different balances, no fixed asset register, and a general ledger nobody can tie back to last year's return. Six months later, someone asks why the balance sheet does not agree with the filed accounts, and the answer costs more than the fee you were trying to improve.

This is the sequence that avoids that, in the order it actually has to happen.

Pick the date before you pick the firm

A handover is cleanest at a boundary the tax year already recognises. In order of preference:

  • 1 April, after the previous year is filed. The closing balances are settled, audited or reviewed if applicable, and become the opening balance set for the new firm. Nothing is in dispute.
  • The start of a quarter, after that quarter's GST returns are filed. Second best, and perfectly workable. Avoid handing over mid-quarter with a return pending — two firms holding half a return each is how deadlines get missed.
  • Immediately, because something is wrong. If filings are being missed or you cannot get a straight answer, do not wait for a tidy date. Move, and accept that the first month will involve reconstruction.

Whatever the date, write it down as a single line in both engagement letters: the outgoing firm is responsible up to and including that date, the incoming firm from the day after. Ambiguity here is where periods get filed twice or not at all.

The handover pack: what to ask for

Ask for this list in writing, from the outgoing firm, before you give notice. Every item is something you are entitled to as the owner of the records, and asking early turns a favour into a scheduled task.

What to ask forWhy the new firm needs it
Trial balance as at the handover dateThe single document the new books open from
General ledger for the current and previous yearLets anyone trace a balance back to the transactions behind it
Chart of accounts, with codesSo categories stay comparable year on year
Fixed asset register with dates, cost and accumulated depreciationDepreciation cannot be recomputed correctly without it
Bank reconciliation statements for the last three monthsShows which items were genuinely outstanding at the cut-off
Filed returns and acknowledgements — income tax, GST, TDSProof of what was actually reported, not what the books say
Payroll register, along with PF, ESI and TDS challansYear-to-date figures drive every remaining month's deductions
Debtor and creditor ageing at the handover dateOpening receivables and payables, name by name
Loan schedules and closing balancesInterest and principal split has to continue, not restart
A data backup in a portable formatInsurance against a login you lose access to later

Two of these are worth insisting on even if the rest arrives late. The trial balance is the document the new books open from — without it, the incoming firm is guessing. The fixed asset register is the one that cannot be reconstructed from bank statements, because the purchase price, the date of first use and the depreciation charged so far are the only things that make next year's number correct.

Opening balances are the whole game

A new set of books is only as good as the figures it starts with. When a handover fails, it almost always fails here: the new firm enters what it was given, the balance sheet does not balance, and a suspense entry quietly absorbs the difference. That entry then sits there for years.

Insist on a signed-off trial balance rather than an exported spreadsheet, and have the incoming firm confirm in writing that it agrees to those balances before the first month is processed. If it does not agree, that disagreement is far cheaper to resolve while the outgoing firm is still answering emails. You can build the opening position yourself with the free Trial Balance and General Ledger tools, and shape the account list with the Chart of Accounts template, which is a useful independent check even when both firms are cooperating.

Then reconcile the bank from the handover date forward before anything else — our bank reconciliation checklist covers the order to work in, and the Bank Reconciliation tool lists the uncleared items for you. If the bank agrees for the first full month under the new firm, the opening balances were probably right.

The professional courtesy that is actually a rule

If both firms are chartered accountants, the incoming CA is expected under the ICAI Code of Ethics to communicate with the outgoing CA before accepting the engagement — the requirement generally cited as Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule. In practice this means a letter, and a reply confirming there is no professional reason the new firm should decline.

You do not have to manage this, and you should not have to chase it. But you should know it exists, for two reasons. First, a new firm that starts work without it is skipping a step, which tells you something. Second, the requirement is about professional conduct, not about your unpaid bills — an outgoing firm cannot use it as leverage. If fees are genuinely outstanding, settle them, because a dispute is a slow and expensive way to hold up your own records. Precisely how this applies to a bookkeeping-only engagement, as opposed to an audit, is a question for the professionals involved.

Credentials and access, not just files

Documents are the obvious half of a handover. Access is the half people forget until it blocks a filing.

  1. Change the password on the GST portal and confirm the registered email and mobile are yours, not the firm's.
  2. Do the same on the income tax portal, and check the registered contact there separately — it is often different.
  3. Check TRACES, the PF and ESI portals, and MCA credentials if you are a company.
  4. Remove the outgoing firm's users from your accounting software and add the new one. If the subscription is in the firm's name, move it to yours before you give notice.
  5. Update the authorised signatory and e-invoicing or e-way bill users if the firm was listed.
  6. Redirect any bank or portal alerts that go to the firm's email.

Do this on the handover date, not after. A portal you cannot log into on the day a return is due turns a routine filing into a week of support tickets.

Keep the old records — longer than you think

Handing the work over does not hand over your obligation to hold the records. Broadly, and subject to your own circumstances: books under the Income Tax Act are generally to be kept for six years from the end of the relevant assessment year; GST records for six years from the last date of filing the annual return for that year; and a company's books under the Companies Act, 2013 for eight years from the end of the financial year. Longer periods can apply where proceedings are open.

The practical version: take your own backup at handover and keep it somewhere you control. Not the outgoing firm's server, not a shared drive owned by someone else's login. Firms merge, close and change systems, and none of that is a defence when records are asked for.

What to agree with the incoming firm

Before the first invoice, get these in the engagement letter rather than in an email thread:

  • Scope by frequency. Monthly bookkeeping, quarterly reviews and annual filings are different jobs. Say which you are buying.
  • What you deliver, and by when. Bank statements, purchase bills and payroll inputs by a fixed day each month. Most delays start on the client side.
  • What you receive, and by when. A profit and loss statement, balance sheet and a short commentary by a stated working day.
  • Who owns the file. Your data, exportable on request, in a named format.
  • Who does the catch-up. If months are missing, that is separate work with its own fee. Agree it upfront rather than discovering it in month three.

If you are still weighing whether to move the work outside at all, our comparison of outsourced bookkeeping versus keeping it in-house covers the cost and control trade directly, and the month-end close checklist sets out what a good monthly rhythm looks like once the switch is done.

The first ninety days

Judge the new firm on three things, not on the fee. Did the first month close on the day it was promised? Did the bank reconcile without a suspense entry? And when you asked a question about a number, did you get an answer that referenced a transaction rather than a reassurance? A firm that clears those three in the first quarter will clear them in year three.

If you want the handover run for you rather than by you, that is what our accounting, bookkeeping and payroll service does — we take the pack from the outgoing firm, agree the opening balances in writing, and close the first month on a stated date.

This is general information, not tax or legal advice. Retention periods, portal requirements and professional obligations depend on your entity type and circumstances — confirm the specifics with your CA before you act on them.
